mcqs.question: Why is assembly considered a near-1:1 view of machine code?
options: Because assembly programs run slower than machine code
Because each assembly line typically corresponds to exactly one machine instruction word
Because assembly is automatically translated into any high-level language
Because assembly and machine code are the same file format
mcqs.explanation: The one-line-per-instruction correspondence is what makes assembly a readable stand-in for raw instruction words. Assembly and machine code run identically (assembly just assembles to it), it isn't translated into high-level languages, and they're different representations (text vs binary), not the same format.

mcqs.question: What happens to a label like `loop:` when the assembly is assembled into a binary?
options: It becomes a runtime variable accessible to the program
It's resolved into a concrete address and doesn't exist as text in the binary
It's stored in the binary exactly as written for the CPU to read at runtime
It's ignored entirely, including by branch instructions that reference it
mcqs.explanation: Labels are a human-readable convenience the assembler resolves to actual addresses; the binary just contains those resolved addresses/offsets. Labels aren't runtime variables, they don't persist as literal text for the CPU to read, and branch instructions absolutely do use the resolved address.

mcqs.question: In the compiled `for` loop example, why doesn't the assembly output contain anything that looks like a distinct 'for' construct?
options: Because the assembler strips out for loops as an optimization
Because `for` is purely source-level sugar that compiles down to ordinary conditional branches and a jump back to a label
Because for loops can only be expressed in machine code, not assembly
Because the example used an unusually old compiler
mcqs.explanation: for, while, and similar constructs are source-level conveniences; at the instruction level they're indistinguishable branch-and-jump patterns. There's no special-case stripping, machine code can't express loops any more directly than assembly can, and this is standard behavior across compilers, not an artifact of an old one.

mcqs.question: What is a pseudo-instruction like `li $t0, 5` ('load immediate')?
options: A real hardware instruction that always executes as a single machine instruction
An assembler-level convenience that may expand into one or more real instructions
A directive that only affects memory layout, never executed instructions
A syntax error that assemblers silently ignore
mcqs.explanation: Pseudo-instructions are conveniences the assembler expands into genuine hardware instructions — sometimes more than one, as with large constants needing lui+addi. It isn't guaranteed to be a single real instruction, it isn't a mere layout directive, and it's valid syntax the assembler processes, not an error.

mcqs.question: AT&T syntax `movl %eax, %ebx` and Intel syntax `mov ebx, eax` both appear in tooling for the same CPU. What's true about them?
options: They perform different operations because operand order differs
They encode the exact same instruction; only the textual notation and operand order convention differ
AT&T syntax is only valid on ARM, and Intel syntax only on x86
One of the two notations is deprecated and no longer produces valid machine code
mcqs.explanation: Both notations describe the identical underlying instruction (move eax into ebx) — the difference is purely which operand is written first and register/immediate prefixes. It's not a semantic difference, both syntaxes are conventionally used for x86 (not split by ISA vendor), and neither is deprecated.

mcqs.question: You're reading a disassembly and see `mov ebx, eax`, mistakenly assuming AT&T conventions. What error do you make?
options: You'd correctly conclude eax is unaffected
You'd swap source and destination in your mental trace, concluding eax was overwritten with ebx's old value instead of the reverse
You'd conclude the instruction is invalid
There's no possible error since both syntaxes always agree on operand order
mcqs.explanation: Intel syntax puts destination first (ebx gets eax's value); reading it as AT&T (source first) reverses the direction entirely, producing a confidently wrong trace. The instruction is valid Intel syntax, and the two syntaxes explicitly disagree on operand order — that's the entire pitfall.
